:::::

::: {.notes}

Writing is where research leaves your head and can first be misread. This
milestone turns your audited results into claims a stranger can weigh: each
one bounded by what the design established, traced to the output that supports
it, and accompanied by an honest account of what AI did along the way. The
discipline is simple and strict. A claim with no row in the evidence table
does not ship.

Milestone 10 adapts these bounded claims to a real audience and rehearses
their defense. The milestone chapter keeps the working details: the practice
steps, the versioned record, and how the artifact is assessed.

## The research decision {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · The research decision"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.decision}

Your analysis printed a number. Now you decide the sentence that number lets
you assert: the headline you will show in public and defend out loud, worded
so its verb stays inside what your design established and its uncertainty
rides in the same eye-span. You choose the words. You lock them. You never let
a tool talk your claim past its boundary.

:::

:::::


## The words this chapter uses {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · The words this chapter uses"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · Key terms

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms .two}

::: {.term}

[Uncertainty in the same eye-span]{.t}

[the interval or caveat sits right beside the claim, not in a footnote (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016).]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Traceability]{.t}

[every number you show walks back to the exact notebook cell that produced it.]{.d}

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Each term is defined in the chapter on first use; these are the definitions as
the book gives them.

:::


## A claim that outruns its evidence makes a judge distrust the whole board {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · A claim that outruns its evidence makes a judge distrust the whole board"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- That is a research-integrity judge, working a poster session.
- She is not testing your statistics.
- She is testing whether your words match the evidence underneath them.

::: {.note-card}

If the headline reads 'lowers blood pressure' but the study only watched who
chose to walk, I stop reading.

:::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Open with the judge, because she is the reader every headline eventually
meets. She points at one number and asks where it came from and what it lets
you say. Ask the room what she would do at their own poster, and let them
answer before you define anything.

:::


## Your analysis prints a number; your headline asserts a sentence {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · Your analysis prints a number; your headline asserts a sentence"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- A result is not yet a claim.
- The gap between the two is where most projects break.
- The sentence almost always wants to say more than the number earned.
- Close that gap yourself, before a stranger finds it open.

:::::

::: {.notes}

State the gap plainly, then say why it is easy to miss from inside and easy to
find from outside. Nobody drafts a dishonest headline on purpose; the sentence
drifts because it almost always wants to say more than the number earned. The
rest of the chapter is a habit for catching that drift before the poster hall
does.

:::


## A result is a number; a claim is a sentence you will defend {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · A result is a number; a claim is a sentence you will defend"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms}

::: {.term}

[Result]{.t}

[a number your analysis produced, such as a difference of 6 points between two group averages]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Claim]{.t}

[a sentence you assert and will defend, such as 'the walking group had lower blood pressure']{.d}

:::

::::

- Turning the first into the second is a decision, not a formatting step.
- You choose how much the sentence is allowed to say.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Both words get used loosely, so pin them down before anything else. The result
is what the analysis printed. The claim is what you will say out loud and
defend when someone pushes back. Because you choose how far the sentence
reaches, this is a research decision that belongs to you.

:::


## The kind belongs to the question; the status belongs to the design {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · The kind belongs to the question; the status belongs to the design"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms}

::: {.term}

[Question]{.t}

[what you set out to learn, and its kind comes from its own words]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Identification status]{.t}

[whether this design can actually deliver that answer]{.d}

:::

::::

- "Does walking lower blood pressure?" asks what an intervention would change, so it is causal.
- It stays causal no matter which data you managed to collect.
- Watched who already chose to walk: not identified by this design, under the assumptions you can defend.
- Your result is then a descriptive association, real and worth reporting.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Four ideas govern the choice, and keeping the first three apart is what stops
overclaiming before it starts. The question's kind comes from its own words,
so weak data never downgrades a causal question into a descriptive one. The
status is whether this design can actually deliver that answer (Blair et al.
2023): if nothing separates the walking from the kind of person who walks, the
status is not identified under the assumptions you can defend. The result sits
beside the causal question rather than replacing it.

:::


## "Causal and unidentified" fuses two fields into one status {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · “Causal and unidentified” fuses two fields into one status"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The status never repeats the word "causal".
- Written as one status, it fuses the two fields you just separated.
- Keep two lines: what the question asks, and what the design delivers.

:::::

::: {.notes}

This is the slip to watch for, and it looks harmless. The kind belongs to the
question and the status belongs to the design, so a status that carries the
word causal is quietly answering the question it was supposed to leave open.
Have someone read their own two lines aloud and check that the lines say
different things.

:::


## Four lines you can reuse on any project {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · Four lines you can reuse on any project"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- **Question kind:** causal.
- **Identification status:** not identified by this design under stated assumptions.
- **Result:** observed association.
- **Claim boundary:** association only.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Put the card on the board and leave it there for the rest of the session. Four
fields, written out, and it travels to any project you will run. When somebody
asks whether a headline is honest, the answer gets read off this card instead
of argued about.

:::


## A defended identification argument is what earns a causal verb {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · A defended identification argument is what earns a causal verb"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.lead}

Your claim boundary lives in the headline verb.

:::

- With no identification argument you write "was associated with lower," never "lowered."
- What earns the causal verb is the argument, not the size of the gap (Hernán & Robins 2020).
- Randomizing is the cleanest way to get one.
- Observational designs can carry causal answers when their assumptions are argued and defended.
- What you may never do is use the verb without the argument.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Read the condition slowly, because it is the whole rule and it is routinely
dropped. The observational-causal pathway earlier in the book shows designs
that do reach causal answers, so this is not a ban on observational work. It
is a requirement that the argument exist and be defended before the verb
changes.

:::


## A bound a reader has to hunt for is a bound doing hidden work {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · A bound a reader has to hunt for is a bound doing hidden work"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Print "about 6 points lower (95% interval: 1 to 11)" under the headline.
- The reader meets the doubt at the same moment as the number.
- The 6-point gap points back to the one line of code that computed it.
- A number you cannot trace cannot go up.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Two habits make the honesty visible rather than merely asserted. Keeping the
interval in the same eye-span means a footnote can no longer carry the caveat
where nobody reads it (Wasserstein & Lazar 2016). Tracing means you can show
the cell that produced the number when a judge asks. Say plainly that the
numbers in this chapter's examples are constructed to make the point, and that
the uncertainty lesson is where intervals get built properly.

:::


## Forty volunteers, a 6-point gap, and a headline that reaches too far {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · Forty volunteers, a 6-point gap, and a headline that reaches too far"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- A small human-physiology pilot: forty volunteers wear a step tracker for a month.
- Twenty walk at least 8,000 steps a day; twenty do not.
- Average resting systolic: 128 active, 134 less-active.
- The draft headline reads "Walking LOWERS blood pressure."
- Two bars on an axis starting at 125, told apart by red and green alone.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Give the setup exactly as the pilot ran, then show the draft board and let the
room list what is wrong with it before you do. Three problems are sitting
there: the verb, the truncated axis, and color carrying the whole comparison.
The result itself, the 6-point gap, is fine.

:::


## The verb claims a crossing the design never paid for {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · The verb claims a crossing the design never paid for"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The question behind this study is causal, and it stays causal.
- Nobody was assigned to walk.
- The active group may differ in age, diet, or baseline health.
- Fill the card, and the honest verb is "was associated with lower."

:::::

::: {.notes}

Walk the decision one field at a time. The question is causal, the design
cannot answer it, and the comparison leaves every group difference untouched.
Those three fields together fix what the sentence may say. Ask the room which
single word changes, and make them say why that word and not the number.

:::


## Where the axis starts is part of the claim {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · Where the axis starts is part of the claim"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Bars encode magnitude, so starting them at 125 makes 6 points look like a cliff.
- Start the bars at a meaningful zero.
- Better: plot the two group averages as points with their intervals.
- Use a blood-pressure scale a clinician would recognize.
- Label each bar with its value, so color is never the only channel.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Figure honesty is part of the claim audit, not a separate design chore. A
truncated axis makes the picture assert more than the number does. On the
labels, say who this is for: a reader who cannot separate red from green, or
who hears the figure read aloud by a screen reader, should still receive the
number rather than only the hue.

:::


## Same result, a claim that survives the judge {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · Same result, a claim that survives the judge"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Nothing about the result changed.
- The verb was downgraded, and the interval rides in the same eye-span.
- A boundary line names what the design does not establish.

::: {.note-card}

In this sample, more-active volunteers averaged about 6 points lower resting
systolic blood pressure (95% interval: 1 to 11); this is an observed
association, and this design does not identify whether walking caused the
drop.

:::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Read the locked claim out loud, slowly. It is longer than the draft headline
and it is the version you can defend when a stranger pushes on it. Point out
that all three repairs are visible in one sentence: the verb, the interval,
and the boundary. Say again that this interval is constructed for the example,
as the chapter states.

:::


## The printout shows the difference the poster never did {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · The printout shows the difference the poster never did"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The volunteers chose how much to walk, and age drives both.
- Watch the two group ages printed beside the 6-point gap.
- The age line is one difference you can see.
- The design leaves every unseen one untouched.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Forty volunteers who CHOSE how much they walk. Age drives both.
n = 40
age = np.r_[rng.normal(31, 7, 20), rng.normal(43, 7, 20)]   # active are younger
active = np.r_[np.ones(20, bool), np.zeros(20, bool)]
systolic = np.round(112 + 0.5 * age + rng.normal(0, 6, n))

gap = systolic[~active].mean() - systolic[active].mean()
print(f"active group mean systolic      : {systolic[active].mean():.0f}")
print(f"less-active group mean systolic : {systolic[~active].mean():.0f}")
print(f"observed gap                    : {gap:.0f} points")
print(f"mean age, active vs less-active : {age[active].mean():.0f} vs "
      f"{age[~active].mean():.0f}")
print("\nnobody was assigned to walk. the age line is one difference you can")
print("see; the design leaves every unseen one untouched, so the verb stays")
print("'is associated with'")
```

:::::

::: {.notes}

Run the block and stop on the last two prints rather than the gap. Age is
visible here only because the example was built that way; in a real pilot you
would not get the list of confounders printed for you. Ask the room what else
might differ between the two groups, let the answers pile up, and land the
point: nobody was assigned, so the verb stays "is associated with".

:::


## An AI failure case {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · An AI failure case"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.failure}

[Where the tool failed]{.label}

You paste your honest headline into a tool and ask it to make it "punchier."
It returns, with total confidence, "Walking Reduces Blood Pressure by 6
Points." It reads beautifully and it is wrong. The tool upgraded your verb
from an association to a cause and dropped your interval, a silent scope
change dressed up as a copy edit.

:::

:::::


## How it failed {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · How it failed"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · An AI failure case

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You catch it by comparing the new verb to what your design earned.
- Your question was causal and stays causal, but nobody was assigned to walk, so nothing identifies that answer and "reduces" claims a warrant you never held.
- You also notice the "6 points" now stands alone with no interval beside it.
- You revert to "was associated with about 6 points lower (95% interval: 1 to 11)." The fluent rewrite reviewed your style; only you can review your claim.

:::::

::: {.notes}

You catch it by comparing the new verb to what your design earned. Your
question was causal and stays causal, but nobody was assigned to walk, so
nothing identifies that answer and "reduces" claims a warrant you never held.
You also notice the "6 points" now stands alone with no interval beside it.
You revert to "was associated with about 6 points lower (95% interval: 1 to
11)." The fluent rewrite reviewed your style; only you can review your claim.

:::


## Do not delegate {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · Do not delegate"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.rule-human}

[This stays yours]{.label}

Three calls stay yours. You choose the **verb in your headline**, the one word
that fixes your claim boundary. You make the **defend-or-concede call** when a
question pushes on that boundary out loud. And you make the **lock decision**:
the judgment that every number is traced, every citation resolves, and the
claim is ready to be final. A tool can draft questions and hunt sources, but
it cannot decide what your evidence licenses or when your claim is earned.

:::

:::::


## It is your turn {data-menu-title="Ch 28 · It is your turn"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 28 · Your move

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

1. List every result you might put in front of a reader, then write the claim sentence each one licenses.
2. Check every verb against what your design established, and downgrade the ones that reach too far. "Caused" becomes "was associated with"; "predicts" becomes "flagged."
3. Write a boundary line beside each claim naming what it does not establish, and put the uncertainty in the same eye-span as the number.
4. Trace every number back to the cell that produced it and cut the ones you cannot walk back.
5. Log it in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one claim with a named method from the [Verification Guide](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/verification-guide.html).

::: {.turn}
Work it in the [companion notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/davi-moreira/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/blob/main/notebooks/book/ch28_from_results_to_claims.ipynb) with [Chapter 28](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part5-communicating/25-from-results-to-claims.html) open beside it. Log every delegation in your AI Research Ledger.
:::

::: {.kicker}

Lesson 2 of this studio · Chapter 29

:::

::: {.divider-line}

for each claim you make, which specific evidence backs it and where that

:::


## The research decision {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · The research decision"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.decision}

For every claim your work makes in public, decide which exact piece of
evidence backs it, where that evidence lives, and what it does not establish.
Then write all three in one row of a claim–evidence table, before the claim
reaches anywhere a stranger can point at it.

:::

:::::


## One vague answer costs you every other number {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · One vague answer costs you every other number"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- A research-integrity judge, working a poster hall, on what one answer decides.
- The doubt does not stay on that number. It reaches every other number up there.

::: {.note-card}

Walk me to the line that made it and I trust the whole poster. Say 'it's in
the analysis somewhere' and I stop believing every other number up there.

:::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Read the judge's line as the scene it is: someone stops in front of your
board, picks a number, and asks where it came from. Notice what the judge says
happens on a bad answer, because it is the part people do not expect. The cost
is not one number marked wrong, it is that every other number on the poster
now looks like the same kind of number. Ask the room which figure on their own
draft they would least like to be pointed at.

:::


## The gap is between a claim you can say and one you can back {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · The gap is between a claim you can say and one you can back"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- A poster is a set of promises made in public.
- Each headline number, each figure, each cited fact: a stranger can test it in ninety seconds.
- A claim-evidence table closes that gap on purpose, before anyone points a finger.
- The honesty is built into the work, not patched under pressure.

:::::

::: {.notes}

The decision on the table is narrow and it is per claim: for each claim you
make, which specific evidence backs it and where that evidence can be found.
Saying a claim is easy and backing it is a separate act, and the whole chapter
lives in the distance between the two. The table is what makes that distance
visible to you first, at your desk, rather than to a stranger in a hall.

:::


## One row per claim, and the row names its own evidence {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · One row per claim, and the row names its own evidence"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- **Claim-evidence table:** a table with one row per claim, pairing each claim with the evidence behind it.
- Claim column: "Store B sold about 1.4 times as many units per week as Store A."
- Evidence column: the two weekly sales averages.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Keep the first pass this plain, because the instrument is genuinely this
simple and its difficulty is elsewhere. The store example is a row cut to its
two core parts: an assertion on the left, the specific thing that produced it
on the right. The next slide adds the other two columns, trace and boundary,
and the rest of the chapter is about them.

:::


## Four columns carry each row, and Evidence is not Trace {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · Four columns carry each row, and Evidence is not Trace"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms .two}

::: {.term}

[Claim]{.t}

[the statement you assert as true]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Evidence]{.t}

[the exact result or source that backs the claim, with its uncertainty]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Trace]{.t}

[where a number was actually produced, named precisely enough to open]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Boundary]{.t}

[the line between what the evidence licenses and what it does not]{.d}

:::

::::

- Claim: "turnout in these precincts was 61.3 percent."
- Trace: "cell 16, where `turnout = ballots.sum() / registered.sum()` runs."
- Boundary: "one county, one midterm election, registered voters only, so this is not the statewide rate."

:::::

::: {.notes}

Take Evidence and Trace as two different jobs, since the room will want to
merge them. Evidence is the result with its uncertainty, which for the turnout
example is 30 sampled precincts giving 48,900 ballots against 79,800
registered voters, plus the interval of plus or minus 1.8 points around the
estimate. Trace is the address where that result was produced, named precisely
enough that someone can open it. The boundary column carries the claim
boundary, the line between what the evidence licenses and what it does not
(ALLEA – All European Academies 2023): here it says that nothing is claimed
about the statewide rate.

:::


## A number you cannot walk back does not belong on the board {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · A number you cannot walk back does not belong on the board"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- **Traceable number:** one you can walk back to the notebook cell that computed it.
- **Untraceable number:** one you cannot walk back, typed from memory or rounded by hand.
- Building the table is the skill, and a blank cell is a visible hole.
- With every claim in a filled row, an unbacked claim has nowhere to hide (Munafò et al. 2017).

:::::

::: {.notes}

The two words are the practical test, and you apply them one number at a time.
Ask of any figure on the board: can I open the thing that made this, right
now, in front of someone. If the answer is that you remember writing it down,
the number is untraceable and the chapter's rule is that it comes off the
board. The blank cell matters for the same reason: the table does not make
weak claims strong, it makes them impossible to overlook.

:::


## You build Row 1 before the file goes to the printer {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · You build Row 1 before the file goes to the printer"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Your political-science poster reports turnout in one county's midterm election.
- Headline: "turnout in these precincts was 61.3 percent."
- Row 1 claim: "turnout was 61.3 ± 1.8 percent."
- Row 1 evidence: 30 sampled precincts, 47,871 ballots against 78,117 registered voters.

:::::

::: {.notes}

The quantity here is the share of registered voters who cast a ballot, in one
county, in one midterm. The interval comes from the spread of the 30
precinct-level rates, so the uncertainty is carried in the evidence column
rather than left off. Row 1's trace is cell 16, the line that divides ballots
by registered voters, and its boundary is one county, one midterm, registered
voters only, so nothing is claimed about statewide turnout or about eligible
adults who never registered.

:::


## The table caught 63.0 before a judge did {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · The table caught 63.0 before a judge did"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You reach for the trace and the draft board reads 63.0, not 61.3.
- You had quietly written the officially reported statewide figure instead.
- Your own cell never produced 63.0.
- Filling Row 1 is what forced the catch.

:::::

::: {.notes}

This is the moment worth slowing down on, because the error is not
carelessness. Two real numbers were in your head, one from your analysis and
one from an official release, and the wrong one reached the board. Nothing
about looking at the poster would have revealed it. Reaching for the trace
did, which is the argument for filling the column at all.

:::


## Row 2 bounds itself: only two definitions were tested {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · Row 2 bounds itself: only two definitions were tested"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Claim: "the estimate barely moves when I change how a registration counts as active."
- Evidence: under two reasonable definitions the estimates differ by less than your sampling spread.
- Trace: cell 18, the definition comparison.
- Boundary: nothing is claimed about looser rolls that keep long-inactive registrations.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Row 2 says the estimate barely moves, and a claim worded that way can quietly
reach past what was tested. The evidence supports a statement about two
definitions, so the claim has to stay a statement about two definitions. Point
at the boundary sentence and ask the room what it would take to earn the wider
version. By the chapter's own boundary, it would take testing the looser
rolls, which is work, not wording.

:::


## Two claims, two rows, every number walked back to a cell {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · Two claims, two rows, every number walked back to a cell"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Every boundary written down, before the file goes to the printer.
- That table is what lets your work survive a pointed finger.
- Tracing every reported claim to the line that produced it is the reproducibility reforms' practical core (Munafò et al. 2017).

:::::

::: {.notes}

Two rows is a small table, which is the point: with one row per claim, the
instrument scales with how much you assert in public, not with how much
analysis you ran. The reproducibility literature asks for this same discipline
at the level of a whole field, and the table is the version of it you can run
on your own poster. Ask each person how many distinct claims their current
poster makes, counting the ones a figure makes without a sentence, and watch
the count come out higher than they expected.

:::


## Run the traced line; that print is the only number Row 1 may carry {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · Run the traced line; that print is the only number Row 1 may carry"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Watch the line marked `# the traced line`. That is the address Trace points at.
- The printed turnout and spread are what Row 1 copies, digit for digit.
- Any board figure this line does not produce is untraceable, whoever published it.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

# Thirty sampled precincts: ballots cast and registered voters.
registered = rng.integers(2300, 3000, size=30)
rate = np.clip(rng.normal(0.625, 0.050, size=30), 0.35, 0.85)
ballots = np.round(registered * rate).astype(int)

turnout = ballots.sum() / registered.sum()                  # the traced line
spread = 1.96 * rate.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(rate)) * 100

print(f"precincts sampled  : {len(registered)}")
print(f"ballots cast       : {ballots.sum():,}")
print(f"registered voters  : {registered.sum():,}")
print(f"turnout            : {turnout*100:.1f} ± {spread:.1f} percent")
print("\nthat is the number your Trace cell must point at. any figure on the")
print("board that this line does not produce is untraceable, whoever published it")
```

:::::

::: {.notes}

Run it live if you can, with SEED set to 464 so the printout is the same for
everyone. Have the room say which printed line feeds Row 1's claim column and
which ones feed its evidence column. Then make the closing point explicit: the
last two printed lines are a rule, not a comment, and an official figure from
a real election office is still untraceable if your own analysis did not
produce it.

:::


## An AI failure case {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · An AI failure case"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.failure}

[Where the tool failed]{.label}

You paste your poster text and ask an AI tool to build the whole
claim–evidence table for you. It returns a clean, complete grid, every cell
filled, and the trace column reads confidently: "turnout value from cell 14."
You almost accept it. Then you open cell 14, and it totals the registered
voters; it never divides. The rate you report is produced two cells later, in
cell 16. The tool guessed a plausible cell number and filled it with full
confidence, and its tidy finished table hid the wrong trace behind a polished
look.

:::

:::::


## How it failed {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · How it failed"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29 · An AI failure case

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You catch it by refusing to trust a trace you have not opened.
- Reading the actual cell, number in hand, is the whole discipline.
- A filled table is not a verified table.

:::::

::: {.notes}

You catch it by refusing to trust a trace you have not opened. Reading the
actual cell, number in hand, is the whole discipline. A filled table is not a
verified table.

:::


## Do not delegate {data-menu-title="Ch 29 · Do not delegate"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 29

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.rule-human}

[This stays yours]{.label}

The **wording of each claim**, the **judgment that a piece of evidence
actually backs it**, and the **boundary each claim carries** stay yours. An AI
can list claims and draft rows, but it cannot open your notebook cell to
confirm a number is real, and it cannot decide the evidence is honest enough
to print. The call that the table is complete and the work is locked is yours
to declare and defend.

:::

## The research decision {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · The research decision"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.decision}

Decide exactly what you will say about every AI tool you used: which tool, on
which task, and how you checked what came back. Then record it, so when
someone asks *"did you use AI, and how did you verify it?"* you answer from a
checkable record instead of from memory.

:::

:::::


## The words this chapter uses {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · The words this chapter uses"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · Key terms

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms .two}

::: {.term}

[AI disclosure]{.t}

[a truthful statement of where and how you used an AI tool in your work (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors 2026).]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Research integrity]{.t}

[the practice of keeping your work honest and traceable, so a reader can see where each result came from and trust it (ALLEA – All European Academies 2023).]{.d}

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Each term is defined in the chapter on first use; these are the definitions as
the book gives them.

:::


## A result I cannot trace is a result I cannot trust {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · A result I cannot trace is a result I cannot trust"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Said by a conference reviewer, standing at your poster.
- The penalty is not for using the tool.
- The penalty is for not being able to say where, and how you checked.

::: {.note-card}

"I am not going to penalize you for using an AI tool. I am going to penalize
you for not being able to tell me where you used it and how you checked it. A
result I cannot trace back to a source and a verification is a result I cannot
trust."

:::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Read the quote aloud and stop on the second sentence, because that is where
the reviewer moves the standard. Using an AI tool is not the thing being
judged here; the ability to locate the use and the check is. Ask the room what
they would answer right now if a stranger asked them where an AI tool touched
their project.

:::


## "Yes, a bit, and it seemed fine" turns good work into an untrustable result {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · “Yes, a bit, and it seemed fine” turns good work into an untrustable result"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- At your research conference, a stranger can ask you the AI-use question.
- Many journals and conferences now ask authors where and how AI tools were used.
- So it is not a formality you can wave off.
- Disclosure is what keeps an honest use of AI honest under questioning.

:::::

::: {.notes}

The failure here is fast and public. One vague sentence at the poster, and the
work stops being checkable in front of the person asking. Point out that the
chapter calls it good work a moment earlier; what changed is what the reviewer
can verify about it. That is why the chapter says this is not a formality you
can wave off.

:::


## One sentence can name the tool, the task, and the check {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · One sentence can name the tool, the task, and the check"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Which tool: the AI assistant you asked.
- For which task: drafting the code behind the coverage ratio.
- How you verified: recomputed by hand before reporting.

::: {.note-card}

"I used Gemini to draft the code that computed my coverage ratio, and I
recomputed that number by hand before reporting it."

:::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Put the finished sentence up before any definition, so the shape is visible
first. It is short, and it still survives a follow-up question, because each
clause points at something a reader could go and check. Ask the room to write
the same sentence for the last thing they delegated, and watch which of the
three parts goes missing.

:::


## Drop any one of the three parts and the disclosure fails {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · Drop any one of the three parts and the disclosure fails"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.lead}

Three parts make a disclosure complete by this book's standard.

:::

- Each part maps to a column in your ledger.
- "I used AI," with no task named, is meaningless.
- A task with no verification is the gap a reviewer is trained to find.

:::::

::: {.notes}

This is a three-part test rather than a spectrum, and the standard is the
book's own. The second failure is the one that still sounds responsible: the
tool is named, the job is named, and nothing says the output was ever checked.
The chapter's own instruction is to check every sentence against a ledger row,
so run that check on your draft before a reviewer runs it on you.

:::


## A complete disclosure is read off your ledger, not written at the end {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · A complete disclosure is read off your ledger, not written at the end"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Your **AI Research Ledger** is a running table with one row per AI use.
- Each row records the task, the tool, your decision, and the verification method.
- You have kept it since you opened it at the start of your project.
- So the disclosure is already written by the time you need it (Munafò et al. 2017).

:::::

::: {.notes}

The ledger is not a new instrument for this chapter. The chapter's claim is
that you have kept it since the start of the project, which is the whole
argument for filling it honestly week by week. Anyone reconstructing a
disclosure from memory at the end is guessing, and the guess is what a
reviewer catches. Ask the room how many rows their ledger holds right now.

:::


## A coverage ratio of 2.0 means the company earned twice what it owed {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · A coverage ratio of 2.0 means the company earned twice what it owed"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You are presenting a business-analytics poster on a public company's debt.
- The question: can it comfortably pay the interest it owes?
- Your headline number is the **interest coverage ratio**.
- That is operating income divided by the interest owed in a year.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Define the ratio before anything else happens, because the disclosure later
has to name which piece of this number came from where. Operating income is
the income figure the company reports; the interest expense is what it owes on
its debt. Keep the definition on the board while you walk through the two AI
uses.

:::


## Two honest AI uses, and neither is safe until it is disclosed and verified {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · Two honest AI uses, and neither is safe until it is disclosed and verified"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- First use: finding the company's reported operating income.
- Second use: writing the short calculation that turns income and interest into a ratio.
- Both are honest uses.
- Honest is not the same as checked.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Neither of these is a misuse, and the chapter says so plainly, which is the
point. The risk is not in delegating the retrieval or the arithmetic; it is in
reporting the result without a record of what was confirmed. Ask which of the
two uses would be harder to check a month from now if nothing was written
down.

:::


## Editorial guidance requires two of the three columns; the third is this book's {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · Editorial guidance requires two of the three columns; the third is this book's"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Current guidance: name which tool you used, and for what purpose (International Committee of Medical Journal Editors 2026).
- Responsibility for accuracy and attribution stays with you.
- A tool can never be an author.
- How you verified is this book's own requirement on top of that guidance.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Be precise about where the rule comes from, because the room will meet both
standards outside this course. The editorial requirement covers the tool and
the purpose and fixes responsibility on the named author. The verification
column is the book's addition, and the chapter gives its reason: a disclosure
that cannot say how something was checked leaves a reader nothing to trust.

:::


## A reported figure and a computed one need different checks {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · A reported figure and a computed one need different checks"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms}

::: {.term}

[Primary-source reading]{.t}

[you opened the company's published annual report and confirmed the operating income the tool gave you]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Alternative code]{.t}

[you recomputed the same number a second way, instead of trusting the AI-generated cell]{.d}

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.notes}

The verification method depends on what kind of thing you are checking. A
reported figure gets checked against the document that reported it; a computed
figure gets recomputed independently. Both names go in the ledger's
verification column, so the row says what was done rather than that something
was done.

:::


## Recompute the ratio by hand and watch it land on 2.11 {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · Recompute the ratio by hand and watch it land on 2.11"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The two inputs are 276 and 131, in USD millions, from the annual report.
- Watch the printed value against the number the AI-generated cell reported.
- The recomputation is the check, and the ledger row records that you ran it.

```python
# The number the AI code reported, recomputed by hand.
operating_income = 276    # USD millions, confirmed against the annual report
interest_expense = 131    # USD millions, from the same annual report
coverage_ratio   = operating_income / interest_expense
print(round(coverage_ratio, 2))   # 2.11 — matches the AI-generated cell
```

:::::

::: {.notes}

Run it live rather than describing it, so the match happens on screen. Point
out that the comment on the income line is doing real work: that figure was
confirmed against the annual report, which is the other row's check. The next
section shows what happens when a disclosure claims a check that no ledger row
backs.

:::


## You read the two rows aloud, and the claim stays bounded {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · You read the two rows aloud, and the claim stays bounded"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The coverage ratio is about 2.1 for this fiscal year.
- Income confirmed against the annual report; the arithmetic reproduced by hand.
- You read a single year of reported results.
- Not a downturn scenario, and not the debt coming due next year.

:::::

::: {.notes}

The reviewer's question gets answered from the record, so there is nothing to
improvise. Note that the boundary is stated in the same breath as the number,
not extracted later under pressure. Ask the room what a listener learns from
the last two lines that the ratio alone would have hidden.

:::


## An AI failure case {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · An AI failure case"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.failure}

[Where the tool failed]{.label}

You ask a tool to "write my AI-use disclosure from these notes," and it hands
back a polished paragraph: *"All AI-generated outputs were independently
verified against primary sources."* It reads beautifully, and it is false. You
verified the operating income against the annual report, but you never
independently checked the interest figure the same tool helped you pull. The
sentence upgraded one real check into a blanket claim of "all."

:::

:::::


## How it failed {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · How it failed"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30 · An AI failure case

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You catch it by reading the disclosure line by line against your ledger.
- Every sentence claiming a verification must point to a row that names that check.
- The word "all" has no such row, so it is fabricated and comes out.
- Your true disclosure is narrower and stronger: you name the two checks you ran and the one input you did not independently confirm.
- A confident paragraph is not a truthful one.

:::::

::: {.notes}

You catch it by reading the disclosure line by line against your ledger. Every
sentence claiming a verification must point to a row that names that check.
The word "all" has no such row, so it is fabricated and comes out. Your true
disclosure is narrower and stronger: you name the two checks you ran and the
one input you did not independently confirm. A confident paragraph is not a
truthful one. You verify the disclosure against the record, not against how
responsible it sounds.

:::


## Do not delegate {data-menu-title="Ch 30 · Do not delegate"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 30

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.rule-human}

[This stays yours]{.label}

The honesty of the disclosure is yours alone. You decide **which uses to
disclose** (including the one you would rather not mention), **whether a
verification you claim actually happened**, and **whether the final statement
is true**. A tool can format your ledger into a clean paragraph. It cannot
know what you really did or certify that you checked it. Signing your name to
a disclosure you cannot back is the integrity failure this chapter exists to
prevent.

:::

:::::

::: {.kicker}

Lesson 4 of this studio · Chapter 31

:::

::: {.divider-line}

which finding leads your written note, and how big each claim is allowed to be
once your voice is no longer in the room

:::


## The research decision {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The research decision"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.decision}

When you turn your research dossier into a written note, decide which finding
has earned the headline and exactly how big each claim is allowed to be given
your evidence, then package the note so a stranger can rerun it and reach your
number without you in the room. Whatever you present along the way — a poster,
a talk, a brief — is one input to that note, never its source.

:::

:::::


## The words this chapter uses {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The words this chapter uses"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · Key terms

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms .two}

::: {.term}

[Working logic]{.t}

[how the dossier and any presentation of it speak: compressed records and, when you present, your live voice filling the silences.]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Paper logic]{.t}

[communication that must stand alone on the page, where every claim is argued in prose because you are not there to answer.]{.d}

:::

::::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Each term is defined in the chapter on first use; these are the definitions as
the book gives them.

:::


## The reviewer wants your most defensible result, not your flashiest {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The reviewer wants your most defensible result, not your flashiest"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The decision: which finding leads, and how big its claim is allowed to be.
- She is asking which finding you would still defend after the room empties.
- And whether she could rerun your work and watch the same number return.

::: {.note-card}

"Show me your results in the order you trust them. If your flashiest number
comes from one lucky run and it leads the paper, I already know how this
review ends. I do not want your most surprising result first. I want your most
defensible one." — a conference reviewer

:::

:::::

::: {.notes}

Read the reviewer's words aloud and let them sit. A big number by itself does
not impress her; she is telling you the order she reads in, and the order is
trust, not surprise. Two questions are hiding in that paragraph, and the
chapter answers both: which finding earns the headline, and could a stranger
rerun the work and get your number back. Ask the room which of their own
results would lead today, and whether they would still lead tomorrow.

:::


## The note has no you standing next to it {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The note has no you standing next to it"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · Why this decision matters

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.lead}

When you present, your voice fills the silences. The page has no voice.

:::

- Every leap a presentation lets you imply, the prose has to earn.
- In order, for a reader who will never hear you explain it.
- Whatever you present is one input to the note, never its source.

:::::

::: {.notes}

This is the whole reason a dossier or a poster cannot simply be retyped into a
paper. Standing next to your work, you answer the objection the moment a face
goes puzzled, so the compressed version survives. On the page nobody asks, so
nothing gets repaired, and an argument with a hole in it just reads as an
argument with a hole in it. Keep the chapter's ordering claim: the
presentation feeds the note, and the note is never a transcript of the
presentation.

:::


## A poster's Gap box says one line; the note argues the paragraph {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · A poster's Gap box says one line; the note argues the paragraph"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Working logic: compressed records, plus your live voice filling the silences.
- A Gap box reading only 'few studies of wait times at peak hours'.
- Paper logic: every claim argued in prose, because you are not there to answer.
- The same gap, written out: what prior work covered, what it skipped, why that matters.
- Turning one into the other is not adding words. It is making the reasoning visible.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Put the two versions of the same gap side by side, because the difference is
the entire lesson. The poster line is not wrong, it is incomplete on purpose,
and you were the missing half. The paragraph has to do the work your voice
did: name the prior studies, say what they left out, and say why the missing
piece is worth anyone's time. Warn against the usual first attempt, which is
padding the poster line with adjectives instead of supplying the reasoning it
never carried.

:::


## Problem, gap, question: the spine holds only when the gap is real {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · Problem, gap, question: the spine holds only when the gap is real"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms}

::: {.term}

[Problem–gap–question spine]{.t}

[the real trouble your work responds to, the specific thing prior retrievable work has not established, and the answerable question that closes exactly that gap]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Evidence density]{.t}

[the share of a paragraph resting on sources a reader could open rather than bare assertion]{.d}

:::

::::

- Problem: customers give up and leave during the morning rush.
- Gap: published wait-time studies measure only quiet, steady hours.
- Question: how much does mobile pre-order cut the wait during the rush here?
- 'As everyone knows' carries no density. A published figure a reader can recompute carries some.

:::::

::: {.notes}

A note carries its reasoning on this backbone (Mensh & Kording 2017), and the
three pieces have to be linked, not merely present. Test the link out loud:
does the question close exactly the gap you named, or a wider one you would
rather answer? The gap is the piece that fails most often, because a gap is
only real once you have shown what is already known. That showing is what
evidence density measures, so a gap paragraph with no openable sources in it
is an assertion wearing a paragraph's clothes.

:::


## Best-supported first, one lucky run last {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · Best-supported first, one lucky run last"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms}

::: {.term}

[Results hierarchy]{.t}

[the order you present findings in, best-supported first and fragile last]{.d}

:::

::::

- A median measured over a thousand simulated mornings leads.
- One unusually fast order waits at the back, labeled exploratory.
- Limitations follow the same discipline, sized to what actually threatens the claim.
- 'Measured on a simulated arrival pattern, not a real Saturday rush.'
- Not a generic 'more research is needed.'

:::::

::: {.notes}

The hierarchy is a claim about trust, so writing it forces you to rank your
own evidence before a reviewer does it for you. The same discipline governs
the limitations section, which is where most drafts go slack: a generic call
for more research costs you nothing and tells the reader nothing. Ask the room
for the one sentence a hostile reader would raise first about their project,
and put that sentence in the limitations rather than the filler one.

:::


## A note a reader cannot rerun is half a claim {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · A note a reader cannot rerun is half a claim"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · The concept

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

:::: {.terms}

::: {.term}

[Reproducibility capsule]{.t}

[everything a stranger needs to rebuild your number and nothing they must guess]{.d}

:::

::: {.term}

[Restart-and-run-all]{.t}

[clear everything, run every cell top to bottom, and the headline number returns]{.d}

:::

::::

- Pinned data and tool versions.
- A fixed seed.
- A decision log.
- Your AI-use ledger.

:::::

::: {.notes}

The chapter is blunt here: readable is only half of the job, and the other
half is runnable (National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine
2019). Take the capsule's second clause as seriously as the first, because the
failure mode is not a missing file, it is a step you did by hand and never
wrote down. Restart-and-run-all is the check that catches it, and it only
counts on a clean kernel, not on the session where everything already lives in
memory (Wilson et al. 2017).

:::


## '38% faster' is a table row, not yet a claim you can defend {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · '38% faster' is a table row, not yet a claim you can defend"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You tested a mobile pre-order option for a campus coffee shop.
- Your claim–evidence table holds the headline row: '38% faster.'
- The note has to turn that row into a claim you can defend.

:::::

::: {.notes}

The row is where your claim–evidence table left you, and it is genuine work: a
number tied to evidence. What it is not yet is a sentence anyone can weigh,
because it carries no setting, no sample and no boundary. The next three moves
are the whole chapter in miniature, so name them before you walk through them:
rank the findings, size the claim, package it.

:::


## The 99% drop is one customer; the 38% is a thousand arrivals {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The 99% drop is one customer; the 38% is a thousand arrivals"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Across a thousand simulated arrivals, median wait dropped about 38%.
- With a tight interval around it.
- One pre-ordering customer was served almost instantly: a 99% drop.
- The median leads. The lone customer goes to the back, as one observation.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Both numbers came out of the same run, and the bigger one is the one you would
most enjoy putting on a slide. That is exactly why the ranking rule exists. A
median over a thousand arrivals is a statement about the procedure; one fast
order is a statement about one morning and one person. Say plainly what the
lone customer is allowed to be in the note: one observation, labeled as such,
not a result.

:::


## Drop 'median' and 'simulated' and you promise what you never tested {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · Drop 'median' and 'simulated' and you promise what you never tested"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Honest: 'on this simulated arrival pattern, mobile pre-order cut median wait by about 38%.'
- Interval attached, and the boundary in the same sentence.
- 'This is a measurement on simulated demand, not a guarantee for a real Saturday rush.'
- Refused: 'mobile pre-order makes the shop 38% faster.'
- That drops the demand pattern, drops median, and promises every customer a shorter wait.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Read the two sentences one after the other and ask the room which one they
would rather write. Most people would rather write the refused one, because it
is shorter and it sounds surer. Then count what the short version quietly
deleted: the arrival pattern it was measured on, the word median, and the
difference between a typical customer and every customer. Writing the refused
version down on purpose is the point of the exercise, since a claim you have
named is a claim you can catch when it creeps back in during editing.

:::


## The capsule is what makes the 38% return on a clean kernel {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The capsule is what makes the 38% return on a clean kernel"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- Pin the simulation's seed.
- Record the machine and library versions.
- Log that you excluded the first order of the morning, and why.
- Pass restart-and-run-all so the 38% comes back.
- The note is now readable and runnable.

:::::

::: {.notes}

Notice that the exclusion is logged with its reason, not just recorded. A
stranger rerunning your work does not need to agree with the choice, but they
do need to see that it was a choice and know what it was for. This is the
point where the note stops being a document about your work and starts being a
thing someone else can operate.

:::


## The printout is already the note's order of trust {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · The printout is already the note's order of trust"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · A worked example

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- The median drop prints with its interval, never on its own.
- The luckiest customer prints at the bottom, where the note puts it.
- The code labels that last line as one observation, not a result.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
SEED = 464
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)

n = 1000
service = rng.gamma(2.0, 55.0, size=n)                  # ordinary counter service
preorder = rng.gamma(2.0, 36.0, size=n)                 # mobile pre-order

med_drop = 1 - np.median(preorder) / np.median(service)
boot = [1 - np.median(rng.choice(preorder, n)) / np.median(rng.choice(service, n))
        for _ in range(2000)]
lo, hi = np.percentile(boot, [2.5, 97.5])
luckiest = 1 - preorder.min() / np.median(service)

print(f"median wait, ordinary service : {np.median(service):.0f} s")
print(f"median wait, mobile pre-order : {np.median(preorder):.0f} s")
print(f"median drop                   : {med_drop*100:.0f}% "
      f"[{lo*100:.0f}%, {hi*100:.0f}%]")
print(f"the single luckiest customer  : {luckiest*100:.0f}% faster")
print("\nthe headline is the first number with its interval. the last one is")
print("one observation, and it goes at the back of the note labelled as such")
```

:::::

::: {.notes}

The block runs the arrivals and prints the ranked findings in the order the
note will use them, so the printout is itself the results hierarchy. Point at
the printed interval and say that the headline sentence has to carry it. Then
point at the last line, which the code labels for you, and ask what would have
to be true before that number could move up the page.

:::


## An AI failure case {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · An AI failure case"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.failure}

[Where the tool failed]{.label}

You paste your discussion into your AI and ask it to make the writing sharper.
It hands back cleaner prose, and it runs through your spell-check without a
flag. Buried in the polish, one sentence has changed size. Your original said
"median wait time dropped about 38% on this simulated arrival pattern." The
rewrite says "mobile pre-order makes the shop roughly 38% faster." The word
median is gone, the demand-pattern boundary is gone, and a measurement on
simulated demand now promises every customer a shorter wait. The sentence
reads better and claims more.

:::

:::::


## How it failed {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · How it failed"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · An AI failure case

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

- You catch it by diffing the rewrite against your original sentence and against your printed result.
- The number came from a median over a seeded simulation, not a mean, and not a real Saturday rush, so the general claim is not licensed.
- You keep the edits that clarify and reject the one that inflated.
- Fluent prose is not evidence.
- You verify the claim, not the polish.

:::::

::: {.notes}

You catch it by diffing the rewrite against your original sentence and against
your printed result. The number came from a median over a seeded simulation,
not a mean, and not a real Saturday rush, so the general claim is not
licensed. You keep the edits that clarify and reject the one that inflated.
Fluent prose is not evidence. You verify the claim, not the polish.

:::


## Do not delegate {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · Do not delegate"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

::: {.rule-human}

[This stays yours]{.label}

Three calls stay yours no matter how fluent the tool is. **Which finding is
your headline**, **how big that claim is allowed to be**, and **which sources
are real** are never delegated. An AI can sharpen a sentence, but a sharper
sentence is not a bigger finding, and clean prose is exactly how an overclaim
sneaks in. You own the words you put your name on, their boundary, and their
uncertainty.

:::

:::::


## It is your turn {data-menu-title="Ch 31 · It is your turn"}

::: {.kicker}

Chapter 31 · Your move

:::

::::: {.slide-body}

1. Write your problem–gap–question spine as three short paragraphs.
2. Order your findings, best-supported first.
3. Write your headline claim in one sentence, with its boundary inside the same sentence: the setting, the sample, and the population it does not cover.
4. Size your limitations to what actually threatens the claim.
5. Assemble the full note, not only its spine: methods (what you did, so a stranger could follow), results with their uncertainty, a discussion sized to the claim, references, your AI-use disclosure placed where the venue expects it, and the pointer to the package Studio 11 will freeze.
6. Attach your folder to the note and confirm the two agree: the number in your lead sentence is the number a cold restart-and-run-all prints.
7. Log the drafting round in your AI Research Ledger, and verify at least one output with a named method from the [Verification Guide](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/verification-guide.html).

Work it in the [companion notebook](https://colab.research.google.com/github/davi-moreira/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/blob/main/notebooks/book/ch31_from_poster_to_research_note.ipynb) with [Chapter 31](https://davi-moreira.github.io/2026F_evidence_driven_research_purdue_HONR464/book/part6-after-conference/33-from-poster-to-research-note.html) open beside it. Log every delegation in your AI Research Ledger.

::: {.note-card}

[How the record works]{.label}

Your milestone artifact is a dated, numbered **version** with the reason for
the version attached. When later evidence changes it, you write the next
version rather than editing the last one, because the sequence of changes is
itself part of your research record.
